title: Statistical Questions and Data
contentObjective: I can tell the difference between a statistical question and a non-statistical question.
languageObjective: I can explain my reasoning using the words statistical question, data, variability, and survey.

noticeAndWonder.context: Look closely at these five national park photographs before you clock in as today's basketball data analyst. Some questions about them have one exact answer no matter who checks — like "How many photographs are shown here?" (five). Other questions would give a different number for every park you asked about — like "How many visitors does each park welcome per day?" or "How tall is each mountain range pictured?" Noticing the difference between a one-answer question and a many-answers question is exactly the skill you'll use in a minute, when you sort scouting questions about a youth basketball team.
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Surveys and Statistics
revealWordProblem.text: Some sixth-grade students want to get more food choices in the cafeteria. They will conduct a survey of students who buy lunch in the cafeteria. What questions should they include in their survey? Explain your choices.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: A good survey question must be a statistical question — one that anticipates variability, since different students will give different answers. Two strong choices: 'On a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied are you with the current cafeteria food choices?' and 'Which new lunch item would you most like to see added: pizza, tacos, a salad bar, or stir-fry?' Both work because the answers will differ from student to student and can be tallied — for example, if 45 out of 80 students surveyed pick tacos, that's 45 ÷ 80 = 0.5625 = 56.25% of respondents, showing tacos as the clear favorite to petition for. A question like 'How many days a week does the cafeteria serve lunch?' would NOT belong on the survey, because it has one fixed answer for every student and doesn't anticipate variability.

turnAndTalk.kernel: A statistical question expects answers that vary across many cases.

turnAndTalk.question: The newspaper editor prefers "How many goals did each player score?" over "How many goals did the team score total?" Which gives more interesting data for a story?

turnAndTalk.extend: Critique the reporter's plan: when might a single total actually be the RIGHT thing to report instead of per-player data? Defend your view.
extendStems: A total would be better when the reader wants to know ___.

extendStems: My rule is: a question is statistical if ___.
I can test any question by asking whether the answers will ___.

turnAndTalk.kernel: If you expect the answers to vary, it is a statistical question.

Some questions will give you interesting data with variety, while others have just one fixed answer. Your job: figure out which questions are worth investigating with data.

conceptIntro.heading: What makes a question a statistical question?
conceptIntro.intro: A statistical question is one you answer by collecting data, and the answers are different for different people or cases. A non-statistical question has just one fixed answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: If you expect the answers to vary, it is a statistical question.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Question 1: "How many points did our top player score last night?" There is one player and one game, so there is one fixed answer, like 18 points.
One answer, no variety, so this is NOT a statistical question.
Question 2: "How many points does each player score per game?" The answers vary: 8, 12, 12, 15, 18, 20, 22.
Because the answers are different for different players, I must collect data. This IS a statistical question.

lines: New question: "How many pets does each student in our class have?" Will every student give the same answer, or different answers?
Some students have 0 pets and others have 2 or 3, so the answers vary. Is this statistical or not statistical?
Now a different question: "How many days are in one week?" Does this have one fixed answer or many?

youDo.title: Now it's your turn
lines: Next, you will sort questions into Statistical or Not Statistical, just like I did.

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How many goals did the league's top scorer net this season?

workedExample.label: Student decision
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: It names only one player, so there can be no variability in the answers.

optional.correctWork: The reason is wrong. "This season" covers many games, and the player scores a different number of goals in each game. Because the data varies from game to game, the question DOES anticipate variability — so it IS a statistical question.
hints: Ask whether the data would have different values across the many games in a season.
Variability can come from many games for one player, not just from many players.

approaching.stem: Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many points did each player score this season?
How many points are scored for a free throw?
What sport does this team play?
How many halves are in a soccer game?
approaching.explanation: "How many points did each player score?" is statistical because different players will have different scores — there is variability in the data.
choiceFeedback: A free throw's points are fixed—does this question ask about variation?
What sport is played doesn't vary—do different people answer this differently?
Halves in a game is a rule—does it change from one observation to another?
hints: Re-read each question and ask: would different people or games give different answers, or is there just one fixed answer?
A statistical question expects variability — many answers that differ. Sort each choice into 'one fixed answer' or 'answers that vary'.
Test one: 'How many halves are in a soccer game?' Every game has the same number — no variability there. Check the other three the same way.

approaching.stem: Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many innings are in a baseball game?
How many home runs did each player hit this year?
How many miles does each runner train per week?
How tall is each player on the basketball team?
approaching.explanation: "How many innings are in a baseball game?" has one fixed answer (9) — no variability. The other questions all produce different answers for different people.
choiceFeedback: Each player hit a different number of home runs—would the answer vary?
Different runners train different miles—would the data vary?
Each player has a different height—would the answers vary?
hints: Careful — this asks for the question that is NOT statistical: the one with a single fixed answer instead of varying data.
For each choice ask: 'Would each player or runner give a different number?' The odd one out is a rule of the game, not data you collect.
Start with 'How tall is each player?' — heights differ player to player, so that one IS statistical. Keep testing until one has just one answer.

approaching.stem: Why is 'How many hours of sleep did each student get last night?' a statistical question?
choices: Because different students got different amounts of sleep
Because it asks about sleep
Because hours are numbers
Because the answer is always 8 hours
approaching.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — different students slept different amounts, so the data will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sleep is a topic, not why it's statistical—which choice describes variability?
Hours are numbers, but are they used only in statistical questions?
If everyone slept 8 hours, would this be a statistical question?
hints: The question asks WHY it's statistical — focus on what happens when many students answer, not on the topic of sleep.
Think: if you asked every student how long they slept, would you get one number or many different numbers? That idea is called variability.
Picture asking 5 classmates their sleep hours and listing the numbers. Notice whether the list is all the same or varied — that's the key idea.

Sort by asking: does this question collect data from many individuals (varies), or state one fact with a single answer (doesn't vary)?

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How tall is each player on the basketball team?

workedExample.label: Student decision
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: Height is just one number, so every answer will be the same.

approaching.correctWork: The reason is wrong. The question asks about EACH player, and different players have different heights — for example 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Because the answers vary from player to player, this IS a statistical question.
hints: The word "each" is a clue that you need data from many players.
Ask yourself: will every player give the same height, or different heights?

onLevel.stem: A coach asks: "How many hours does each athlete on the track team sleep the night before a meet?" Why is this a statistical question?
choices: Because the answers will vary from athlete to athlete
Because it is about sports
Because it has a numerical answer
Because the coach asked it
onLevel.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability. Different athletes sleep different amounts, so the data collected will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sports is a topic—what specific part makes this statistical?
Numbers can appear in fixed-answer questions too—why is this different?
Who asks the question doesn't determine if it's statistical—look deeper.
hints: Notice the words 'each athlete' — the coach plans to collect one number from every runner on the team.
Ask: will all athletes report the same hours of sleep? What we call it when collected answers differ is the key to this question.
Imagine the coach's list: 8, 6.5, 9, 7 hours from different athletes. The first step is naming what a changing list like that shows.

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How many points does the team need to win a game?

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: It is about basketball and the answer is a number, so it must be statistical.

onLevel.correctWork: The reason is wrong. Being about basketball or having a number does not make a question statistical. "How many points does the team need to win a game?" has one fixed answer — you only need to score more than the other team — so the answers do not vary. This is NOT a statistical question.
hints: Numbers and a sports topic do not automatically make a question statistical.
Ask whether the answers would VARY. If there is one fixed answer, it is not statistical.

onLevel.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: What time is it right now?
How tall are the students in my class?
What is my shoe size?
What is 7 × 8?
onLevel.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — students' heights differ, so the data will vary.
choiceFeedback: What time it is right now doesn't vary—would collecting data help here?
Your shoe size is one fixed measurement—does it vary for different people?
Multiplication has one answer—would this question ever need data?
hints: Three of these have exactly one answer you could look up or compute. Find the one where collecting data from many people makes sense.
For each choice ask: 'If I surveyed my whole class, would I get a list of different numbers?' A statistical question needs that variety.
Test 'What is 7 × 8?' first — it has one answer no matter who you ask, so it can't be statistical. Apply the same test to the rest.

onLevel.stem: Which of these would collect data that VARIES (making it a statistical question)?
choices: How many days are in one week?
How many siblings does each student in the class have?
How many minutes are in one hour?
What is 12 + 12?
onLevel.explanation: Number of siblings varies from student to student, so the collected data will vary — that makes it statistical. The others each have one fixed answer.
choiceFeedback: Days in a week is constant—does it vary?
Minutes in an hour don't change—does it vary?
12+12 always equals 24—would data vary?
hints: The capital word VARIES is the clue — you need the question whose answers change from student to student.
Check each choice: is it a fact of the calendar, clock, or math (never changes), or a survey where classmates would answer differently?
Start with 'How many days are in one week?' — that never changes, so its data can't vary. Keep testing each choice the same way.

workedExample.work: How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?

workedExample.label: Student says

extending.stem: A survey asks 30 students how many books they read last month, collecting 30 answers. What makes this a statistical question?
choices: It is about books
Everyone reads the same number
The answers vary from student to student
It has exactly one correct answer
extending.explanation: Statistical questions anticipate variability in the data collected across many people.
choiceFeedback: A topic doesn't determine if a question is statistical—what else matters?
If everyone read the same number, would this be statistical?
One answer means fixed, not statistical—but do the answers vary here?
hints: Re-read the setup: 30 students each report how many books they read — that's 30 separate answers collected.
Ask what those 30 answers probably look like: all identical, or a mix like 2, 5, 0, 7...? That property is what makes a question statistical.
First step: picture the list of 30 numbers. Decide whether the list is fixed or full of different values, then match that idea to a choice.

extending.stem: Which rewrite turns 'What is my resting heart rate?' into a statistical question?

What is a heart rate?
What is the teacher's heart rate?
What are the resting heart rates of students in my class?
extending.explanation: Asking across many people, whose rates vary, makes the question statistical.
choiceFeedback: This still asks about one person—does one person's answer vary?
This still asks about one person—will the answer vary?
One person's rate doesn't vary—will you get different answers?
hints: The original question asks about ONE person's resting heart rate — one measurement, so no variability.
A statistical rewrite must gather data from many people whose numbers differ. Check each choice: how many people does it measure?

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Statistical Questions and Data is judging a question by its topic or its numbers instead of its variability. Students see a question about ONE player, ONE game, or ONE fixed fact — like "How many points does the team need to win a game?" — and call it statistical just because it has a number or is about sports. Or they see a question about a single player's whole season, like "How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?", and call it NOT statistical because only one player is named, forgetting that a season covers many games with a different result each time. Both errors skip the real test: will the answers actually differ from case to case (game to game, player to player)? If yes, it is a statistical question; if there is one fixed answer, it is not.

connect.scenario: The school newspaper wants to write a story about the girls' soccer team. A reporter suggests asking: "How many goals has the team scored total?" The editor says they should ask: "How many goals did each player score this season?"
connect.promptQuestion: Which question is statistical? Why would the editor's question give the newspaper more interesting data?
connect.prompt: The reporter's question is ___ because ___. The editor's question is ___ because ___. The editor's question is better for a story because ___.

exitTicket.stem:
Which question is a statistical question?
A) How many students are in the school?
B) How many hours does each student in 6th grade exercise per week?
C) What time does school start?
D) How many days are in a week?
choices: B) How many hours does each student exercise per week?
A) How many students are in the school?
C) What time does school start?
D) How many days are in a week?
exitTicket.explanation: "How many hours does each student exercise per week?" is statistical because different students exercise different amounts — the data has variability.
choiceFeedback: That has one exact answer — statistical questions expect varied data.
One fixed time isn't statistical — look for varying answers.
That's always 7 — statistical questions have answers that vary.
hints: Look for the question where you'd collect a different number from each 6th grader instead of looking up one fixed fact.
Sort the four options into 'one fixed answer' vs 'answers that vary.' Only one belongs in the 'varies' group — that's the statistical one.
First step: try option D — days in a week never changes, so it has no variability. Apply that same check to A, B, and C.
